en: You named him Külchoro.
He felled all who faced him;
You made him a hero who shook the world.
Yet unable to overcome one vicious dog,
Almighty Kydyr and the one God,
You made him equal to the black earth—
Why did you diminish him so?
When we were created, O one God,
We were helmets of crimson steel,
The Kyrgyz people’s glorious bloom.
We charged like lions,
And hissed like dragons,
Thick-armed and stone-hearted.
We cast the world into great turmoil,
Wearing eighty-four pieces of armor;
Wherever we struck, crimson fire arose.
We readied ourselves like hawks,
And subtle wisdom came to us.
We were descendants of the dark gray wolf,
Who guarded the Ala-Too and made it home,
And disgraced all who fought us.
Were we not towering peaks and mountain passes,
Hardened by spilling blood,
Renowned for breaking the enemy—
Descendants of the dark gray wolf,
The plain where a nation might encamp,
The sons of gray-maned heroes?
He was the spring of the jagged mountain,
Almambet’s finest champion.
Never before had an enemy
Dared advance upon Talas,
Nor had any man prevailed against it.
When we desired glory against the cunning foe,
Was this a night when honor should perish?
Was this a day when Sarybay, the ogre’s son,
Would enter and possess Talas,
And subject it to disgrace?
O almighty God of majesty,
We thundered like blue steel,
And all who saw us shuddered.
He became the hero Külchoro,
Külchoro mounted his horse,
He climbed towering into the saddle,
Subduing the whole wide world,
Driving and ruling wherever he went.
He crossed many a formidable pass,
He struck the enemy in many lands.
Unless his appointed hour had come, he did not die,
An infidel such as this
He had never seen in all the world.
He girded himself for the encounter,
Swaying as though struck by a peri.
He readied his Jazayil sword,
And prayed to the Creator;
It was too late to turn uphill,
And, eager to face his foe,
His two eyes became four.
Then the lionhearted choro
Roared straight ahead,
And raised the battle cry of Manas;
He thrust his sword into its sheath,
And appealed to the spirits
Of the heroes who had passed into eternity.
His adversary was Sarybai,
A foe as mighty as a mountain.
Sarybai mounted Jooruker,
Riding jauntily without a care;
He counted neither your choro nor any other,
And did not value the eighteen thousand worlds
As much as the hem of his robe—
Such was the madman's nature.
“I am Sarybai,” he said,
“The eighteen thousand worlds
I shall gulp down like a dragon,
Driving them before me and devouring them.”
He grew furious and worked himself up,
And spoke to Külchoro,
Beginning his savage rage.
Gulping like a dragon,
He had overwhelmed all the world;
None who opposed him remained alive,
And he had laid waste the valleys.
Whenever he came in bitter enmity,
He even destroyed his own kin.
He prepared himself and sharpened his steel,
And crushed the people of Kanghai.
He had ridden on campaign to Altai,
And received the old lion’s blessing.
Wherever he had camped in passing,
A sacred shrine arose,
And hosts of holy men supported him.
Wherever he had spent the night,
A deep-rooted plane tree grew,
And God raised a protecting cliff at its roots.
He sprang from a lineage of saints;
The one confronting him was Sarybai—
Could he stand without facing him?
Would God strike him if he held back?
The one he grappled with was Sarybai—
Could he stand against such a struggle?
He was the heir of the lamented Lion;
Would God strike him if he fled?
On the promontory where armies gathered,
Upon the rounded hillock,
On the saddle of the forked pass,
On the flat ground broad as a palm,
Upon the ridge where armies massed,
Sarybai, son of a monster,
At the place where they faced each other—
By the echoing Jar-Kyya,
Along the slopes of Jan-Moinok—
Against the infidel huge as a cliff,
Your hero choro was about to contend,
Against the warrior Sarybai.
He met Sarybai, skilled and deft with the spear,
Mighty in wielding the sword,
He met Sarybai,
The infidel who had roamed there.
The hero choro was about to contend
Against the warrior Sarybai.
“Upon the beauty who cannot be won by asking,
I shall cast my cruel lasso.
After battling you, I shall drag your beauty
From your very embrace.
I am a cool pavilion on the heights;
I am the warrior Sarybai.
Seven giants beneath the earth
I devoured single-handed.
The mighty giants upon the earth
I drove before me and swallowed.
Defiant khans
I crushed beneath my heel,
And scattered their blood like water.
Still unsated with blood,
I am the warrior Sarybai.
Finding no mountain to strike,
Finding no enemy to fight,
Finding no stone for my teeth,
Finding no head to tear away,
I am a bloodthirsty butcher never sated with blood;
Every worthy rival who faced me died,
And I am one of the measureless heroes.
Though I gulp and drink blood,
My thirst remains unquenched.
I am fury itself,
The black eye of the dread destroyer.”
So saying, Sarybai
Struck Jooruker once upon the flank,
Took the blue spear in his hand,
And roared in fury;
The wretch stood against him.
When Sarybai leveled his spear,
His menace split heaven and earth;
When he stood there enraged,
Could the hero-born Külchoro
Draw back even from stone,
Or turn away from death?
He rejoiced at the word “death,”
Revealing himself a lion.
The lionlike, vigilant man
Swooped straight upon him.
Sarybai, son of a monster,
Charged like a boar.
He sprang like a tiger;
Those who clashed with him did not survive.
He arranged all his weapons,
And the cast-iron head, broad as a room,
Of this infidel was made ready.
He had brows like a crouching hound,
And a head as large as a cauldron;
His two cheeks hung loose,
As though two Dungans had eaten their fill.
Upon the infidel’s two shoulders,
It seemed two great birds had perched.
He roared in fury,
Calling all the khans
To come before him:
“Do not come alone—come in pairs!
Do not come one by one—come all together!
I shall strip away your strength
And spill your blood like a spring!
Now I shall take your life,
And make your blood flow like water.
Come with your khan Semetey at your head!
Let no regret remain within you;
Come, all of you, and harbor no regrets.
Let the warrior Seytek come as well,
Let Argyn and Kyrgyz come together.
I shall erase every trace of you,
And smash to splinters
Your villages set in a circle.
I shall seize as my true prize
Your wife, the lovely Aichürök.
Your heroes and your khans—
I shall slaughter you all.
Without quarrel or strife,
Submit to what I say.
Enchanting beauty Aichürök,
If you do not obey my words,
If you do not surrender Aichürök,
Behold, your choro stood thus,
Seeming like a sheer blue mountain.
His Surkon beneath him,
He wheeled about, leveling his spear;
The steed he rode against the foe
He gripped tightly with his thighs.
Its shaft was steel and its point was keen,
A decorated spear with a tasseled tip,
Shining there in his hand.
Such was the nature of that ornate spear.
From a cluster of barberry on Opol Mountain,
It had been torn out by the roots.
The accursed, ill-fated wood
He had strongmen twist;
So that a sword could not cut through it,
He had it wound with black wire,
And bound with sinew.
He had it covered in mare’s hide,
And had Bölökbai fit the haft;
So it would not slip from the hand,
He had its handgrip grooved.
So it might last for many years,
He had craftsmen decorate it.
He had it leveled at the opposing foe,
And had a tassel fixed to its point.
A master beyond all masters,
He had befriended the prophet David:
The lame smith Bölökbai—
The hero Bölökbai had made it.
They strove and strove,
He and David taking counsel together.
When it came to working the bellows,
A levy was laid upon the Kyrgyz,
And bull-calves were slaughtered.
When it came to making charcoal,
Whole forests were destroyed.
He forged and drew out its point,
And, so that everyone it struck
Might writhe and die,
He tempered it in human tears.
He was a masterful man against the foe.
Subduing the whole wide world—
Was he not the choro accustomed to that?
Punishing the whole world—
Was he not the choro who had done so?
Born into this world—
Was he not the choro who had come?
The keenest of sages,
His eyes could see afar.
He had slain multitudes in many conflicts,
And emerged alone from the contest.
His strength was extraordinary,
And he was famed as the sharp-witted child.
That Külchoro was a lion;
How many giants who faced him
Were leveled with the black earth!
